label: CA firm capacity planning
overview: Capacity planning in a CA or advisory firm is the structured process of aligning available fee earner hours to the current and projected client workload — identifying surpluses and deficits before they become operational crises. The three capacity models (base capacity, scenario versioning, and client trimming) address different planning horizons and problems. Base capacity answers 'where are we now?' Scenario versioning answers 'what happens if we grow, shrink, or restructure?' Client trimming answers 'which clients are consuming capacity that should be redeployed?' All three must be run before any staffing or structural decision is made.

diagnostic_entry.primary_question: Is the capacity challenge a current-state measurement problem (the firm does not have clear visibility of available vs. committed hours), a future-state planning problem (a growth or restructuring decision requires modelling multiple scenarios), or a client portfolio optimisation problem (certain clients are consuming disproportionate capacity relative to their fee contribution)?
diagnostic_entry.current_state_measurement: Run the base capacity model first. Establish total available hours, actual utilisation by staff level, and WIP quantum by service line. This baseline is the prerequisite for any other capacity planning work — scenario modelling is meaningless without an accurate starting position.
diagnostic_entry.future_state_planning: Once the baseline is established, build the scenario version models. Scenarios should include at minimum: the status quo trajectory, a growth scenario (e.g. 20% WIP increase), and a structural change scenario (e.g. partner retirement, new service line, merger). Each scenario reveals different capacity requirements and informs staffing and investment decisions.
diagnostic_entry.client_portfolio_optimisation: If the base model reveals that overall capacity is adequate but certain fee earners are overloaded, run the client trimming analysis. Identify clients whose fee-to-hours ratio is below the firm's target return — these are candidates for fee renegotiation, service reduction, or managed exit. Releasing low-value client hours creates capacity for higher-value work without increasing headcount.

materials.name: Base Capacity & Job Estimation Model
materials.summary: Sets the baseline assumptions — how long jobs take, who performs them, and what that costs at each staff level and charge-out rate. It calculates job costs dynamically and exposes skill deficiencies, most usefully the moment expensive senior people are absorbing junior work because the lower tier is too thin. Past known fees can be aligned against projected assumptions so the model stays grounded in what the firm actually bills.
materials.who_when: Any professional service firm wanting to understand its true baseline capacity, validate chargeable targets, or work out why staff feel overworked when the totals say there is enough time.
steps: Determine how many hours an average, a small and a large job takes.
Select which team member performs each task from the dropdown, so cost follows the level actually doing the work — Junior, Senior, Equity Partner.
If family-group clients distort the compliance statistics, override the total client count with the actual number of returns filed.
Enter past known fees and apply seasonal adjustments — the model assumes a perfect world, and the adjustment is what brings adjusted capacity back into a realistic range.
If you are mid-year, change the period tracker (for example to 10 periods) so actual-versus-planned tracking stays accurate.
Review the skill levels tab for the telling bottleneck: upper-level team members with spare capacity while the tiers below them have none.
Read that pattern for what it is — highly paid staff stepping down into lower-rate jobs, which halves the effective charge-out rate.
Map fee ranges and client service categories such as Growth, Protect and Transition to discuss where the team should actually be deployed.

materials.name: Scenario Versioning & Management Model
materials.summary: Keeps every what-if inside one file rather than a sprawl of near-identical spreadsheets. Scenarios are saved through native version history — "Base Scenario", "Under a thousand clients" — variables changed in the blue cells, and earlier versions restored to compare outcomes. Views are customisable, so a smaller partnership can hide unused partner rows and dashboards rather than scrolling past them.
materials.who_when: Firms of varying partnership size, particularly under six partners, who want to model what-if scenarios aggressively without creating a cluster of disorganised files.
steps: Hide unused partner rows and unnecessary dashboards if the firm has fewer than six partners.
Use the filter range on the fee spread page so each partner sees only their own clients while entering fees.
Have each partner clear the filter, select themselves, enter their data without scrolling the whole firm, then select all again when finished.
Save the current state through File then Version History, and name it plainly — Base Scenario, Trimmed Base.
Change only the variables in the blue cells so it stays obvious what was altered.
Adjust the number of periods where the firm is tracking mid-year, so volatility graphs and capacity ranges calculate correctly.
Use restore to toggle between versions and compare outcomes side by side rather than copying the file.

materials.name: Client Trimming & Advisory Transition Model
materials.summary: Answers the oldest objection in advisory — "we want to do it, but we don't have the time". It models dropping a defined percentage of the lower tier: how many clients, exactly what fees are lost, and precisely how many hours come back. Those hours are then reallocated to higher-margin advisory work, which turns dropping clients from a frightening idea into arithmetic, and often ends in higher profit from fewer working hours.
materials.who_when: Firms trapped in a high-volume compliance cycle, losing margin to senior staff doing junior work, and wanting to pivot to higher-value advisory.
steps: Save the current state as a version first, so the base scenario survives whatever you try next.
Go to the client trimming section and select a percentage of bottom-tier clients to drop — the bottom 10%, for instance.
Read what the model returns: the number of clients affected, the precise fee loss, and the exact hours freed.
Reallocate those recovered hours by adjusting the advisory percentage for partners, associates and senior managers.
Compare the resulting hours and fee potential against the base version rather than against impressions.
Frame the decision on the three pillars — Capacity freed by the trim, Capability meaning the templates and skills are ready, and Opportunity meaning the larger clients willing to engage.
Treat the output as a scenario, not a report: the value is in projecting assumptions, not in historical accuracy.

advisor_guidance.data_quality_determines_model_quality: Capacity planning is only as reliable as the time recording data it is built on. A firm that does not have consistent, accurate daily time recording cannot build a meaningful capacity model — the first intervention must be time recording compliance, not the analytical framework. Do not build the model on unreliable data and present it as fact.
advisor_guidance.scenario_modelling_changes_partner_behav: The most significant value of scenario modelling in a CA firm is not the output — it is the change in how the partnership discusses capacity. Partners who have seen the modelled impact of a partner retirement or a 25% growth scenario make fundamentally different resourcing decisions than partners who are operating on instinct. The model creates a shared evidence base that depersonalises what would otherwise be subjective debates.
advisor_guidance.client_trimming_requires_courage: Most CA firms know intuitively which clients are unprofitable but avoid acting on it because the relationship history, the discomfort of the exit conversation, and the short-term revenue impact feel more concrete than the long-term capacity benefit. The client trimming analysis converts the intuition into data, and the data makes the action possible. The advisor's role is to hold the data in front of the partnership until the decision is made.
advisor_guidance.capacity_planning_is_a_discipline_not_a_: The firms that benefit most from capacity planning are those that embed it as a quarterly discipline — not those that commission a one-off capacity review and shelve the model. The implementation process is designed to install the discipline, not just deliver an analysis. Measure the embedding success by whether the capacity dashboard is being reviewed monthly 12 months after the engagement.
